name: Cyproheptadine
lead: Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine that also blocks serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and has anticholinergic and sedating effects. It is approved for allergic conditions such as seasonal and perennial rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis and urticaria [2][3]. Increased appetite and weight gain are recognised effects of the drug, and it is prescribed off-label as an appetite stimulant, particularly in children with poor weight gain [3][4].

In appearance communities it is discussed mainly as a weight-gain aid, a category the wiki files under muscle. No published trial has tested it for cosmetic or bodybuilding goals in healthy adults. Trial registrations exist for its use against weight loss in children with cancer and in feeding disorders [5][6][7].

Reported adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and urinary retention, and, rarely, liver injury and blood disorders. The US label warns about overdose in children [2][3].
infobox: Rx in US/Canada; OTC in UK; Schedule 3 in Australia (varies)

paras: The US label lists perennial and seasonal allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, mild urticaria and angioedema, cold urticaria, dermatographism, and adjunctive therapy in anaphylaxis [2]. In the UK and some other countries it is also labelled for migraine prevention [3]. Off-label uses include serotonin syndrome, insomnia, antipsychotic-induced akathisia and cyclical vomiting in infants [3].

Weight gain observed in patients during allergy treatment led to its off-label use in underweight children, including those with cystic fibrosis or failure to thrive [3][4]. Reference sources describe the effect as arising from antiserotonergic action, although the mechanism is not fully established [3][4]. A Wikipedia summary notes that the weight-gain literature includes a systematic review and a placebo-controlled trial but does not make the strength of evidence clear [3].

Common effects are sedation (often transient), dizziness, confusion and restlessness, along with anticholinergic effects including blurred vision, constipation, dry mouth, urinary retention and fast heart rate [2][3]. Rare serious effects include liver injury, blood disorders and anaphylaxis [3]. The label warns that antihistamine overdose in infants and children may cause hallucinations, central nervous system depression, convulsions and death, and that effects add to those of alcohol and other sedatives [2]. Contraindications listed in reference material include narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention and concurrent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use [4]. The label places the drug in pregnancy category B [2].

Cyproheptadine is a potent H1 receptor antagonist and also strongly blocks 5-HT2 receptors, with anticholinergic, antidopaminergic and local anesthetic activity; it crosses the blood-brain barrier [3]. It is well absorbed orally, peaks after about 1 to 4 hours, is highly protein bound and is mainly metabolised in the liver [3]. It has been explored as an antagonist of serotonergic psychedelic effects, with inconclusive results [3]. Studies of serotonin in locomotion and spinal injury cite cyproheptadine as a serotonin-receptor antagonist tool in laboratory work [8][9].

Cyproheptadine was patented in 1959 and introduced for medical use in 1961 [3]. Use as an appetite stimulant followed early observations of weight gain in pediatric allergy patients [4]. It is sold worldwide, and in 2023 was the 234th most prescribed medication in the US [3].
No studies have tested cyproheptadine for cosmetic weight gain or muscle building in healthy people.

Registered clinical trials examine it in medical contexts: a completed phase 2 trial of cyproheptadine and megestrol to prevent weight loss in children with cancer cachexia [5], two terminated pediatric cancer trials of weight loss prevention [6][10], a terminated trial in pediatric feeding disorders [7], and COVID-19 and ADHD trials unrelated to appetite [11][12]. Results of these registrations are not summarised in the registry entries cited here.

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use for allergic conditions [3].

lore.intro: Cyproheptadine is mentioned only occasionally on looksmax.org, in discussions drawn from Ray Peat-inspired supplement circles rather than as a dedicated weight-gain protocol [1].

claims.claim: Cyproheptadine, combined with pregnenolone and clonidine, lowers stress and addresses ADD.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread reposts a post by a Peat-community writer recommending a combination of pregnenolone, clonidine and cyproheptadine for stress and low motivation, arguing the immediate problems should be addressed first [1].
claims.experts: The US label lists only allergic indications for cyproheptadine [2]. No published trial of this combination for stress or attention problems is cited in the label or reference summaries reviewed [3].

claims.claim: Cyproheptadine is a useful appetite stimulant for gaining weight.
claims.believers: Off-label prescribers and patient communities describe using it for poor appetite, particularly in underweight children [4].
claims.experts: Increased appetite and weight gain are recognised effects, and pediatric trials have been registered, but use in healthy adults for cosmetic purposes has not been studied [3][5].

card.summary: An allergy antihistamine prescribed off-label for appetite in children; never tested for cosmetic weight gain.
card.note: Sedating and anticholinergic; overdose is dangerous in children. Rx in US and Canada, OTC in the UK.

quick.overview:
Cyproheptadine is an older antihistamine approved for allergies. Because it also blocks serotonin receptors, it increases appetite, and doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label to underweight children.

In appearance forums it comes up as a weight-gain aid and in supplement-stack discussions. No trial has tested it in healthy adults for cosmetic purposes.
quick.mechanism: It blocks histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and also has anticholinergic and sedating effects. Its appetite effect is attributed to blocking serotonin signalling, though the mechanism is not fully settled.
quick.risks: Common effects are drowsiness, dizziness and dry mouth. Rare liver and blood problems are reported, and overdose in children can cause convulsions and death. It is prescription-only in the US and Canada and over the counter in the UK.
